data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Bridges are physical objects subject to material fatigue; theories are logical constructs subject to logical falsification","Bridge testing aims for safety assurance; theory testing aims for knowledge growth via error elimination"],"overturn_conditions":["If the goal of science were defined as 'practical success' rather than 'error elimination', the analogy would fail","If 'severity' could not be objectively determined without referencing past success rates"],"shared_structure":["Selection of the component under highest stress for continued monitoring","Goal is to find failure points quickly, not to prove the component will never fail","Preference for the 'tested' component is strategic, not a belief in its invincibility"],"source_memory_refs":["bridge_stress_testing_protocol"],"transfer_claims":["Just as engineers monitor the most stressed bridge part to learn its limits fastest, scientists should adopt the most tested theory to learn its flaws fastest","Preferring the stressed part does not imply believing it won't break; preferring the corroborated theory does not imply believing it is true"]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-inductive methodological rule to maximize the severity of future tests (falsifiability), accepting the cost that this preference offers no rational guarantee of practical success or truth approximation.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the chosen 'better-corroborated' theory fails a new test while a less-corroborated rival survives, the methodological rule must still be considered valid because the goal was rapid error exposure, not finding the surviving theory.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a scientist prefers a theory because they believe it will work in practice (pragmatic success), they have left Popper's framework and smuggled in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severity' relies on past regularities to predict future test outcomes, the argument collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism reinterprets 'preference' strictly as a decision-rule for theory selection aimed at accelerating error elimination. By choosing the theory that has survived the most severe tests (highest empirical content), scientists select the theory that is currently most vulnerable to falsification. This does not assume the theory is true or probable; it assumes only that testing this theory yields the highest potential information gain. The preference is thus a strategic move within the game of science to expose errors faster, consistent with the goal of falsification rather than verification.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
